questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Location and the University's reputation

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Easy. There is one week of orientation for visiting and transfer students, so you are overloaded with information the first week. Not very useful, however, if you have any questions there are so many people who can answer them during this week.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We received the keys to our accomodation upon arrival, and could ask residential life any questions. Later that same day we had dinner with the International Students Services, who were also helpful to tell us about the orientation program. If anything, they give you too much info and too much assistance.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Too time consuming to spend a week on orientation. They could have sent us a long document, and cut the program down to one day.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Very easy. VISP students have to be housed through Barnard. In December you submit a prioritized wishlist for which buildings you would like to stay in, which can be both off or on campus. They give you your room assignments shortly before arrival in January.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
I stayed in 600 W 116th st and it was really great. The apartments were large, however they are almost all doubles. If you want a single, don't put 600 W as your first priority. Most off campus buildings are 1-5 min away from campus. They all have 24/7 security. You should know that you can request a roomie, so if you know some of the other danish students going, you can request each others and live together. Can be easier than taking the chance of getting a 19 year old american. 
The housing that I expertienced as nice was 1) Sulz tower 2) 600 W 116 3) 616 W 116. The others I haven't seen, but I wouldn't recommend the ones that are a bit further from campus, as you really come to appreciate being right next to campus and the subway

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: While I do think the housing facilities are suprisingly nice, you may be unlucky and end up in a suite with girls who never cleans, so I would be a bit proactive in the beginning about making a cleaning schedule and buy supplies together etc.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Course registration and the shopping period was a bit tricky. Get help from your academic advisor and talk to your NSOP leaders during orientation - they can help you.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You can in december register ONLY for classes at Barnard. Around the 7th of January you can register for all classes, however most will be full, so you will have to jon to waitlist. You can join a max of 3 waitlists and 19 credits of classes in total. Join all the classes you may attend during shopping. Don't stress if you are number 50 on the waitlist, they move a lot during shopping. Everyone always ends up getting the classes they want, unless there are special restrictions. 
Tips: do your course search in vergil and focus onBarnard classes first, as you register for those first. Later look at Columbias. Register as soon as you can, mostly if there's a waitlist so you are higher up. Attend all your waitlisted classes, as they often take attendence, and you can talk to the professor about giving you priority.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You have your own academic advisor that can help. You can contact the registrar for more technical issues.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Got all the ones I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Talk to students about what classes or professors they liked. Look up your professors on culpa to see what students say. Attend as many classes as you can during shopping. Know that you can take basically any class offered at Columbia, even at the different grad schools, although you will need to contact professors directly about registering for classes level 5000+. They don't inform yoy about this beforehand, so I thought our options were limited based on Barnards website, but you can take any course you can find on Vergil basically. 
Try a class that is different from your field of study! They offer insanely many different courses, take advantage of that.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Two classes were third year undergrad, two were graduate or 4th year undergrad.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Much smaller lectures and professors are more available -more office hours etc., and students really take advantage of the OH. Instead of class style lessons with TA's like at UCPH, the TA's often offered either office hours or recitations, but they were more so based on questions from students or going over assignments than actually working through lecture material. A lot more work during the semester with graded assignments, graded participation and both a midterm and final exam.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Money and Banking (would not recommend with Tri Vi Dang)
Finance and the Real Economy  (Would recommend)
Women and Health (would not recommend)
Game Theory (would recommend as a substitute for micro 3)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: See above

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Expect to pay Barnard 100.000 DKK in advance for housing, health insurance and meal plan. Further I spent around 8000 on my own insurance, and around 4.000 on flights in advance. Be aware of this, as it's a lot to pay all at once before leaving, so make sure you save up for that.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Everything is more expensive than at home, but that was to be expected. I was mostly shoicked by how much Barnard charges for housing, insurance and meal plans and over there I was shocked by the insane prices of basic groceries. Eating and drinking out isn't that much more expensive than cph.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They offer a ton of options

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are many clubs and societies you can join. Your student ID also gives you access to many museums in and around NYC, which saves you a ton of money.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to all the museums that are available to you for free!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! You can bring guests! While you are often let in for free, your guests will be let in on pay-as-you-wish, so they can literally give 1 dollar.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Explore! Go out as much as you can, even if it's just a walk in a park or a coffee in a diner. I expected to visit other cities as well, but ended up feeling like 4 months in Manhattan wasn't enough, as there are do many places to visit. Also take advantage of how nice Columbia's campus is.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Relatively easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: They are very welcoming. If you want to make local friends it's super easy.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Americans are very different than danes, so probably people's behavior. Also the food in the dining halls was a bit hard to get used to.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How welcoming and warm Americans are

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Be prepared for lots of paper work in advance, be prepared to pay around 150.000 DKK for the whole thing and please consider how the Trump administration is dealing with international students at the time of your visit and if you are willing to live with the stress of that.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: They shoud send you some sort of enrollment package after your enrollment is confirmed. This contains important deadlines about payment, signing up for classes, uploading vaccination documents, signing up for housing etc. They forgot to send it to us, so the three months before departure were extremely stressful, as we were constantly blindsided by short deadlines. So make sure you receive this enrollment package, if not ask for it.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Living in NYC - 100% worth the struggle and the cost.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I stressed a lot about getting my courses pre-approved by UCPH because I couldn't get the syllabi for the classes until after I was enrolled in them, so that was a bit stressfull. Be prepared for the stress of that, and decide with yourself if you think it's worth it.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: If you are ocnsidering going to Barnard - do it! It's expensive and takes alot of time in preparation, but it's worth it!! However, be sure to check up on the US' policies for student visas, and be prepared for UCPH not helping you with anything. Connect with your fellow UCPH students before going, it's much easier if you help each others.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
